findings.element: first-run state, KPI row, the "haven't moved in a fortnight" card (movementTwo via kpi({ n: D.sitting })), driven at ?state=first-run
findings.problem: On first-run the account is three days old (F.accountDays = 3) and the oldest open job is 3 days (scopes['first-run'].oldest). The surface knows this and acts on it in one place: D.showsFortnight resolves false, so the fortnight rule is deliberately not drawn on the strip, on the stated grounds that a rule no mark can reach reads as a rule every mark has beaten. Two hundred pixels above that suppressed rule the same threshold is printed as a result: a 34px "0" under the heading "What's quietly slipping", captioned "haven't moved in a fortnight", with a meter drawn against the shared denominator of 9. The identical argument applies and is not applied. The other three cards do not have this property - an overdue date or an unowned job can genuinely exist on day three, so their zeros are readings; this one is arithmetically forced.
findings.consequence: The state a new owner is guaranteed to meet first opens with a health check whose headline number cannot be anything but zero, and reads as "nothing has stalled on me". The owner is given credit for fourteen days of discipline they have not had the chance to fail at, on the one screen whose entire job is to tell them whether they are actually on top of it or just busy. The hero directly beside it refuses a comparison it has not earned and names the date it arrives; the card next to it takes the opposite position on the same evidence.
findings.fix: In kpi(), accept a `notYet` reason alongside `unavailable`. In movementTwo, pass it to the sitting card when D.showsFortnight is false (the flag already exists and is already computed from D.fortnight > D.axisMax). A not-yet card keeps its place, its glyph and its numeral 0, drops the meter (a share of a denominator that cannot move is not a reading), and replaces the meter slot with a label-voice line "Nothing has been open that long yet". Its spoken line becomes "0 jobs haven't moved in a fortnight, of 9 jobs open - no job on this account is older than 3 days." Reuse the existing not-available slot markup; introduce no new colour, weight or card shape.
findings.assertion: For state=first-run: the card whose caption contains "fortnight" has no `.meter` element, contains the text "Nothing has been open that long yet", and its `.sr` text names the oldest job's age; and for every state, `document.querySelector('.fortnight') === null` implies that card carries the not-yet treatment - i.e. the number of cards drawn as a plain zero reading is 0 whenever the fortnight rule is suppressed.

findings.element: .fortnight span ("A fortnight") in the ages strip, quiet state, all widths; worst at 390
findings.problem: The label is positioned `left: var(--gap-tight)` off a rule placed at `calc(var(--x) * 1%)` and never flips. In the quiet state the axis maximum derives to 15 and the fortnight sits at 93% of the strip, so the label runs off the right-hand end. Driven: at 1440 and 1280 it overhangs the strip by 24px and stops exactly on the card's border (label right 1289, card right 1290) with none of the 24px padding every other element in that card respects; at 768 it clears the card by 30px; at 390 it clears the card by 55px, is painted on the page ground outside the white card, and is then guillotined by .scroll's `overflow-x: hidden` - the phone shows "A FORTN". Two gate rules look adjacent to this and neither covers it: "no chart label leaves its card" reads the week chart, "no age tick leaves the strip" reads `.strip-scale`. This is not a fixture edge - it triggers whenever the oldest open job is near a fortnight, which is the ordinary case the strip is built to show.
findings.consequence: In the state where the owner is being told everything is fine, the single mark that gives the strip its meaning - the line that separates recent from sitting - is unnamed on a phone. The reader sees a dashed vertical rule near the right edge and a clipped word floating outside the card, and has to guess whether it is the threshold, the axis end, or a rendering fault. It also breaks the card's own margin at desk width, where the label is the only thing on the surface touching a border.
findings.fix: In the existing relayout pass (which already measures the strip after layout and again on fonts.ready and resize), measure the fortnight label's box against the strip's box; when its right edge would exceed the strip's right edge, set `data-flip` on the `.fortnight` element, and add `.fortnight[data-flip] span { left: auto; right: var(--gap-tight); }`.
findings.assertion: For every state and every declared viewport, in both grounds: `.fortnight span`'s bounding box is fully contained by `.strip`'s bounding box (left >= strip.left and right <= strip.right), and its text is never visually clipped (scrollWidth <= clientWidth + 1).

findings.element: .xaxis on the first-run chart (.plot.solo), all widths
findings.problem: `.plot.solo` narrows `.cols` and `.baseline` to 57px and re-anchors `.bar-val`, but `.xaxis` is untouched: it keeps `justify-content: space-between` and its single `span` keeps `flex: 1 1 0; text-align: center`, so the one date label centres itself in the whole chart column. Driven at ?state=first-run: the column's centre is 608 and the label's centre is 905 - the only date on the chart stands 298px to the right of the only mark it names (298px at 1280, 238px at 768, 109px at 390). The same layout leaves 631px of the hero card's 688px evidence column empty at 1440, so a reader's eye crosses two-thirds of a card of white to reach a date that belongs to a column behind them.
findings.consequence: A new owner's first chart reads as broken. There is a hatched bar at the far left and a date floating in the middle of a white field with nothing under it, so the two objects that should be one fact do not look related - and the reader cannot tell whether the date names the bar, names something that failed to draw, or names the empty space itself. This is the state that has to earn the surface's credibility, and it is the state where the layout most obviously has not been composed.
findings.fix: Give the solo chart the width its plot has. Add `.chart:has(.plot.solo) { flex: 0 0 auto; align-self: start; }` (or set the hero grid to `minmax(220px, 300px) auto` when the solo plot is present), plus `.plot.solo ~ .xaxis { width: 57px; padding-right: 0; }` with its single span at `flex: 0 0 auto; text-align: center`. The tick then stands on its column, and the hero's text column takes the slack instead of the card carrying dead width.
findings.assertion: For state=first-run at every declared viewport: |centre(.xaxis span) - centre(.plot.solo .colw)| <= 4px, and the `.chart` element's width is within 8px of the `.plot.solo .cols` width.

findings.element: .xaxis span in the twelve-week chart, in the two thinned bands (max-width 1140 and min-width 901; and max-width 792)
findings.problem: At full density the twelve spans are `flex: 1 1 0`, so each label centres on its own column. In the thinned bands the media query switches the three survivors to `flex: 0 0 auto` inside a `space-between` row, so they are distributed by the container instead of standing on their values. Driven, offset of a tick's centre from its column's centre: at 1140 "8 Jun" is 23px left of column 7 against a 49px column pitch; at 792, 23px; at 768, 22px against a 47px pitch; at 390 all three are off - "27 Apr" +13, "8 Jun" -12, "13 Jul" -13 against a 25.7px pitch, i.e. every visible label on the phone is displaced by half a column and centres on the gap between two bars. This is the mechanism the panel already killed on the age axis in round 1 (ticks stand on their values rather than being spread by flexbox); it survives untouched on the week axis.
findings.consequence: On a phone the label naming the running week - the one column the reader is looking for - sits over the boundary between the last two columns, so the finished 6 Jul week and the unfinished 13 Jul week are equally plausible readings of it. In the 1024-1140 band and at 768 the mid-chart label lands nearly half a column away, so a reader pinning a date to a bar picks the wrong bar or gives up and reads shape only. The chart's whole claim is that twelve specific weeks are drawn; three labels that do not stand on the weeks they name withdraw it at three of the four widths this ships at.
findings.fix: Stop hiding and re-flowing. Keep all twelve spans at `flex: 1 1 0` in the thinned bands and switch the ones that would collide to `visibility: hidden` - the mechanism `.xaxis span.mute` already uses - instead of `display: none` with `flex: 0 0 auto`. In the `(max-width: 1140px) and (min-width: 901px), (max-width: 792px)` rule, replace `display: none` with `visibility: hidden` on the non-survivors and `display: block; flex: 0 0 auto` with `visibility: visible` on first, 7th and last, leaving the flex basis alone.
findings.assertion: For state=full at every declared viewport and in both grounds: for every `.xaxis span` whose computed visibility is not hidden and whose display is not none, |centre(span) - centre(the .colw at the same index)| <= 4px.

findings.problem: The loading composition is the real composition with its ink removed, which is right for geometry and wrong for values. Driven at ?state=loading: the twelve skeleton bars carry the fixture's own `--h` (42, 25, 50, 33, 58, 42, 67, 50, 50, 67, 42, 100) and render at seven distinct heights in the fixture's exact shape, and the nine skeleton dots carry the fixture's real `--x` ages. The plot is a fixed 168px box with absolutely positioned columns, so bar height contributes nothing to layout - the varying heights buy zero geometric stability and publish the reading instead. The gate's skeleton rules all measure containers (card count, hero height, card height, no shimmer, no invented section); none looks at a mark's magnitude.
findings.consequence: A screen that announces "Loading this reading" is legibly showing the reading: the twelve-week shape is readable, and the tallest column is unmistakably the last one, so the answer to the page's question is on screen before the page claims to have it. Either the marks then change under the reader when the real data lands - the surface contradicting itself, which this file spends its whole architecture avoiding - or they do not, in which case the loading state was never loading. In the shipped product this cannot be built at all without the data it is waiting for.
findings.fix: In the loading branch, after the skeleton DOM is built (beside the existing pass that strips `.sr` lines and neuters controls), overwrite the magnitudes: set every `.sk-wrap .bar` to `--h: 46` and space every `.sk-wrap .dot` evenly across the axis in `--x`, then re-run deswarm. Geometry, wrap points and column count are untouched, because none of them depended on the values.
findings.assertion: For state=loading at every declared viewport: the set of distinct rendered heights of `.sk-wrap .bar` has size 1, and the sequence of `--x` values on `.sk-wrap .dot` is evenly spaced and does not equal the sequence derived from LATELY_FIXTURE.scopes.full.jobs ages.

findings.element: a.kpi in the KPI row - the three status cards that are links (full state); the same shape in partial and first-run
findings.problem: Each card's spoken sentence lives in a `.sr` span inside the link, and the visible numeral (.t-num) and phrase (.t-small) beside it are neither aria-hidden nor referenced - the glyph and the meter are hidden, these two are not. A link takes its accessible name from its contents, so the name is the concatenation. Driven and read back: "3 haven't moved in a fortnight 3 jobs haven't moved in a fortnight, of 9 jobs open"; "2 past the day they were due 2 jobs past the day they were due, of 9 jobs open"; "1 has nobody's name on it 1 job has nobody's name on it, of 9 jobs open". The gate asserts every interactive element HAS a name and that no `.sr` line is buried under aria-hidden; nothing asserts the name is said once.
findings.consequence: A screen-reader user tabbing the row hears every count and every phrase twice, three cards running, with the bare fragment arriving first and the sentence second - so the fact registers before the grammar that makes it a fact. The carefully authored spoken line, which exists precisely so the row is not read as loose numerals, is prefixed by the loose numerals.
findings.fix: Add `aria-hidden="true"` to the `.t-num` and `.t-small` spans inside kpi()'s `body` template (both the known and the unavailable branches, and the "Not available" label), leaving the `.sr` span as the sole contributor to the name. The lead card is a div in reading flow and its `.sr` line adds a fact rather than repeating one, so it is left alone.
findings.assertion: For every state and both grounds: for each `a.kpi`, its computed accessible name, whitespace-normalised, equals its `.sr` textContent exactly - no numeral or caption fragment appears twice in the name.

findings.element: ICON.nobody, the square glyph on the "has nobody's name on it" card, ?v=dark
findings.problem: The four status glyphs hard-code their hues in the SVG strings (`stroke="#4f46e5"` and the rest), so they alone do not take part in the ground flip. The dark twin exists in part because Indigo 600 on a near-black ground reads as a bruise, and steps `--accent` to Indigo 400 - every other indigo mark on the surface (the live column, the meter fills, the old dots, the focus ring, the bar value) takes that step; the status square does not. Measured against the plate it actually paints on (`--wash` over `--paper`, #202023): the indigo square renders at 2.58:1, below the 3:1 floor for a mark that carries meaning, while its three neighbours sit at 5.6, 4.7 and 4.7. The audit gate reads text colour against the composited backdrop and does not walk SVG stroke attributes, so nothing sees it.
findings.consequence: On the dark ground one of the four status categories loses its mark: the square is barely separable from its own plate, so a row that should read as four distinct kinds of slippage reads as three plus a blank. The file's stated rule is that status wears a shape as well as a colour and never a colour alone - here it wears a shape nobody can see, which is the same failure from the other end.
findings.fix: Make the glyphs take the ground flip: change the four status SVGs to `stroke="currentColor"` and set the colour on the wrapping `.glyph` with a per-status custom property drawn from the existing tokens - amber, red, `var(--accent)` (which already resolves to Indigo 400 in dark) and emerald. No new hue and no new weight; the light ground renders identically because `--accent` is Indigo 600 there.
findings.assertion: For state=full at ?v=dark: every `.kpi .glyph svg [stroke]` resolves to a colour whose contrast against the composited background of its `.glyph` is >= 3.0:1, and no SVG on the surface carries a literal hex stroke that differs from the value the same token resolves to in the current ground.

findings.element: .dot focus behaviour at 1440x960, the frame width this surface is shot and graded at
findings.problem: `.dot` carries no `scroll-margin`, so focusing the first mark scrolls the container the bare minimum. Driven: seven Tab presses from load move `.scroll` by 4px of the 664px available and leave the dot's bottom at exactly 960 - the window's own bottom edge. Its focus ring (`outline: 2px` at `outline-offset: 3px`) extends to 965 and is clipped by 5px, and the objects that give the mark its meaning are below the fold: the strip axis ends at 954 and the entire scale, "today / 15d / 30d / 45d", occupies 963 to 980, off-screen. The tooltip is placed above the mark, so the job's name is readable; where the mark stands is not.
findings.consequence: A keyboard user arrives at the ages strip and finds a 12px dot pinned to the bottom edge of the screen with its ring cut off, no ruler underneath it, and no way to tell 2 days from 41 days except by reading nine tooltips one at a time. The strip's single idea - that the finding is the tail, and position on the axis is the fact - is unavailable to the one reader who has to move through it mark by mark.
findings.fix: Add `scroll-margin-bottom: var(--gap-hall)` and `scroll-margin-top: var(--gap-room)` to `.dot`, so focusing any mark brings the axis, the scale and a rung of clearance with it. Both values are existing rungs on the declared ladder; nothing else moves.
findings.assertion: At every declared viewport, for each `.dot` in turn under real Tab presses: after focus settles, the dot's focus ring box (its rect inflated by outline-offset + outline-width) is fully inside the viewport, and `.strip-scale`'s bounding box is fully inside the viewport.

findings.element: #retry in the error state (and the same shape on the empty state's "Open Tasks")
findings.problem: The error state designs three of its four parts - the heading names the source, the sentence explains the refusal, the button offers the one move - and does not design the fourth. Driven: clicking #retry changes nothing measurable. The root's markup is identical before and after (3048 characters both times), the URL is unchanged, no live region fires, the console is silent, and the only difference is that the button now holds focus. There is no pending treatment, no disabled interval, no announcement, and no second state for "asked again, still nothing".
findings.consequence: The owner presses the one control on a screen that has just told them their work is unreadable, and gets no answer at all. They cannot distinguish a retry that ran and failed again from a button that does nothing, so the next move is to press it repeatedly and then leave - and the surface's whole argument, that it will tell you plainly when it does not know something, is spent on the one screen that most needed it.
findings.fix: Give the retry its states in the master: on press, set the button to a reading treatment (label "Reading again", `aria-disabled="true"`, pointer events off) and announce it through the same `role="status"` line the loading state already uses; after the attempt, either render the resolved state or return to the error card with the label "Try again" plus one line in the existing note voice - "Asked again at 09:16. Tasks still did not answer." No new component: the button, the note block and the status line all exist.
findings.assertion: For state=error: activating #retry by keyboard and by pointer changes the button's accessible name or its aria-disabled state within one frame and writes text into a live region; and the error card renders a second, distinct treatment after a failed retry rather than markup identical to the first.

findings.element: shell(): the `.reading` line in the header and the `Read` item in the `.coverage` footer, every state
findings.problem: The header stamps "READ AT 09:14, THURSDAY 16 JULY 2026" and the provenance strip at the foot of the same page stamps "READ 09:14, THURSDAY 16 JULY 2026" - the same string in the same uppercase mono voice, differing only by the word "at". Driven across all seven states and all four widths, the count of elements owning that text node is 2 every time. The file's own comment for the reading line says the instant is printed once, at the top, in the label voice; the gate's rule for it asserts `anchored >= 1`, so it can never see a second.
findings.consequence: The one fact everything relative on the screen resolves against is stated twice in two slightly different grammars, which invites the reader to check whether they are the same instant. It is small, but it is the exact class this surface is otherwise strict about, and the provenance strip is where a reader goes once they have started to doubt the numbers.
findings.fix: Drop the `Read` item from the `.coverage` footer. The strip's job is which source answered and which figures are lab-authored; the instant already has an owner at the top of the page. If the strip needs an anchor of its own, make it a relative one in its own voice - `Read this morning` - so the two are not the same sentence twice.
findings.assertion: For every state and both grounds: exactly one element on the surface owns a text node containing LATELY_FIXTURE.readingLong.

findings.element: quiet state, the "Nothing is sitting" card's body sentence
findings.problem: The full state's band counts four conditions - hasn't moved in a fortnight, past the day it was due, nobody's name on it, waiting on something else. The quiet state replaces all four cards with one sentence, and the sentence names three: "All 9 open jobs have moved inside a fortnight, none is past its day, and every one has a name on it." The fourth, waiting on something else, is zero in the quiet scope and is simply not mentioned. The band's own principle is stated in the code beside it - the band does not vanish, because an absent band reads as a bug - and the same reasoning applies one level down, to a category that vanishes from the sentence that replaces it.
findings.consequence: An owner who has learned the four kinds of slippage from the full state reads the all-clear and finds only three of them cleared. The most natural reading of a missing item in a list of four is that it was not checked, which is the one impression this surface works hardest not to give.
findings.fix: Extend the sentence to enumerate all four in the row's order: "All 9 open jobs have moved inside a fortnight, none is past its day, every one has a name on it, and none is waiting on anything else." Keep the existing singular branch for D.open === 1.
findings.assertion: For state=quiet: the `.center .t-body` sentence contains one clause for each of the four status keys in the scope (sitting, overdue, unowned, waiting), matched by the same phrase stems the KPI captions use.

biggestWin: Compose first-run as its own state instead of the full state with pieces taken out. It is the only state a new owner is guaranteed to meet, and it currently carries three separate failures at once: a fortnight card printing a zero that no three-day-old account could make non-zero, sitting directly above a fortnight rule the same code suppresses for exactly that reason; the chart's only date label standing 298px away from the chart's only mark; and 631px of the hero card's 688px evidence column left empty, so the composition reads as a layout that broke rather than a surface that is honestly early. Fix those three together and the surface's central claim - that it will say plainly what it does not yet know - is finally true on the screen where a first-time owner decides whether to believe it. That is a day of work: polish and one small build, not a different decision.
